title: Active Current Mirrors
intro: A current mirror used as a differential pair's load turns a differential input into a single-ended output with no loss of gain.

blocks.text: An NMOS pair (M1, M2) with tail source M5 is loaded by a PMOS mirror (M3, M4). The current change in M1 is mirrored into M4's drain, where it adds to the current change of M2; the output current is twice what a single side would deliver, so the full differential gm appears at a single-ended output.

blocks.source:
Gm = gm1 (= gm2)
Rout = ro2 || ro4
Av = gm1 * (ro2 || ro4)

items: Large-signal: the output node must stay between the saturation limits of M2 and M4, giving a limited but useful swing.
Common-mode: the mirror load makes the stage naturally balanced, and the common-mode gain is small when the tail resistance is large.
The mirror node (drain of M3) introduces a second, 'mirror' pole and zero at about gm3/Cmirror, which matters in high-speed designs.

blocks.text: This circuit, an 'operational transconductance amplifier' (OTA), is the heart of countless op amps and comparators.

blocks.title: OTA gain
blocks.text: gm1 = 1 mS and ro2 = ro4 = 50 kohm. Find the voltage gain.
solution: Rout = 50k || 50k = 25 kohm. Av = gm1 * Rout = 1 mS * 25 kohm = 25.

blocks.title: Why twice the current?
blocks.text: Explain why the mirrored output current is twice that of a single-ended pair.
solution: For a differential input +v/2 and -v/2, M1 current rises by gm*v/2 and M2 falls by gm*v/2. The mirror reflects M1's increase into the output node as an increase, while M2's decrease subtracts from the output node's current. The two changes add: total output current is gm*v, versus gm*v/2 for a pair with one-sided resistive loads.
blocks.answer: Both halves contribute: the mirror inverts one half so the signs add.
